note: Original editorial descriptions written from publicly reported facts (never copied from the Michelin Guide or reviews). Point-in-time; verify before treating chef/menu specifics as current.

addison-san-diego-ca.text: San Diego's first three-Michelin-star restaurant, Addison sits on a Carmel Valley hillside inside the Fairmont Grand Del Mar, its dining room framed by high ceilings and arched windows. Chef William Bradley builds a ten-course, season-driven menu that runs French technique through California ingredients, with playful turns — a churro filled with chicken liver, Kennebec chips with burnt-onion dip and a caviar-topped china sunflower, shellfish chawanmushi. A 10,000-bottle cellar of small producers and rare Champagnes rounds out one of the country's most polished tasting-menu experiences.

benu-san-francisco-ca.text: When Corey Lee opened Benu in 2010, it became the first San Francisco restaurant to hold three Michelin stars. In a minimalist 40-seat SoMa room, Lee gives Asian cooking a French-precise, deeply technical spin — the kitchen's famous "thousand-year-old" quail egg, a lobster-coral xiao long bao with tissue-thin skin, whole roasted quail glazed in maple and soy and carved tableside. Korean and Chinese ideas meet exacting classical technique in a menu that helped redefine modern American fine dining.

carino-chicago-il.text: Tucked beneath the Red Line tracks in Chicago's Uptown — next door to a hair salon — Cariño is chef Norman Fenton's love letter to Mexico. Fenton fell for the country on a nine-month road trip and later ran the kitchen at WILD Tulum; here he channels that immersion into a 12-to-16-course Latin-American tasting menu with a heavy Mexican accent, served to just seven seats at the chef's counter. It opens with a wink — "chips and salsa" reimagined as salsa verde jelly and tortilla crumble — and only gets bolder. A Michelin star, a Banchet Best New Restaurant award, and a James Beard nod have followed; night owls can catch the late-night taco omakase, Wednesday through Saturday at 9:30.

holbox-los-angeles-ca.text: Inside Mercado La Paloma, a former garment factory turned South LA market, Holbox is the country's only Michelin-starred Mexican marisquería. Chef Gilberto Cetina — a three-time James Beard nominee — draws on Mexico's coasts, especially the Yucatán, working sustainably sourced Southern California seafood with lime, tomato, habanero and cilantro. Ceviches of rockfish and kanpachi, wild Mexican shrimp served in a goblet, a velvety red seafood stew and the signature octopus taco have made this counter one of Los Angeles's most beloved tables.

kasama-chicago-il.text: Opened in 2020 by chef-partners Genie Kwon and Tim Flores, Kasama made history as the first Filipino restaurant in the United States to earn a Michelin star — and now holds two. In Chicago's West Town it leads a deliberate double life: a counter-service bakery by day, turning out Filipino pastries and breakfast plates, and a reservation-only tasting menu by night. Kwon's acclaimed pastry work and Flores's savory cooking drive the $325 dinner, with wine or non-alcoholic pairings, which has also earned a James Beard Award and a place among North America's 50 Best. Equal parts neighborhood bakery and long-planned destination, it rewards a casual morning pastry as much as a milestone dinner.

le-bernardin-new-york-ny.text: Born in Paris in 1972 and transplanted to New York in 1986, Le Bernardin has spent decades as the city's definitive seafood restaurant, holding three Michelin stars under chef Eric Ripert. The kitchen honors the fish above all: an à la carte menu organized into "Almost Raw" and "Lightly Cooked" refuses to force guests into a marathon tasting. Signatures like the pounded-thin yellowfin tuna laid over toasted baguette and foie gras distill Ripert's philosophy — French technique, global inspiration, and the purity of the ingredient.

lilo-carlsbad-ca.text: Lilo earned a Michelin star within ten weeks of opening in 2025 — a near-unheard-of ascent for a 22-seat Carlsbad newcomer from chef Eric Bost and restaurateur John Resnick. Bost draws on the Southern California coast, with detours through France, Japan and other kindred coastal cuisines, across a $265 menu of many small, meticulous courses rather than large plates. Dishes like spot prawns in a sauce of sea buckthorn, lime leaf, serrano and gooseberry show the kitchen's precise, produce-driven hand.

mutra-north-miami-fl.text: In a North Miami strip mall, Mutra made history as the first kosher restaurant anywhere to earn a Michelin star. Named for chef Raz Shabtai's late grandmother, it channels the multicultural food traditions of Jerusalem — with threads from North Africa, Eastern Europe and the Levant — into a frequently changing, farm-to-table menu served at an intimate chef's counter. Inspectors singled out its "One Perfect Falafel," a beet dish set in ajo blanco with beetroot sorbet, the signature lamb kebab with smoked eggplant cream, and a rosewater muhallebi to finish.

the-french-laundry-yountville-ca.text: Thomas Keller's French Laundry has anchored American fine dining from its Yountville stone cottage since 1994, holding three Michelin stars for progressive American cooking rooted in classic French technique. Its opening sequence is close to sacred: "Oysters and Pearls," a sabayon of tapioca pearls with poached oysters and caviar, is a course that never changes. Keller's farm-to-table, regional-sourcing ethos set a template that much of the country's high-end cooking still follows.

yingtao-new-york-ny.text: Named for owner Bolun Yao's grandmother, YingTao is the only Michelin-starred Chinese tasting-menu restaurant in New York — a star earned within a year of its 2023 opening by the husband-and-wife team of Bolun and Linette Yao. In a Hell's Kitchen room of black marble, brass and scarlet cherry accents, chef Emily Yuen — a James Beard semifinalist whose résumé spans Michelin kitchens in London, Australia and Singapore — reframes Chinese cooking through contemporary fine dining. The seasonal seven-course, $150 menu trades takeout clichés for philosophy, technique and storytelling.

smyth-chicago-il.text: The passion project of husband-and-wife chefs John Shields and Karen Urie Shields — alumni of Alinea, Tru and Charlie Trotter's — Smyth turns three decades of experience toward North American farmers, fishermen and makers at the peak of their season. In the West Loop, the daily-changing $420 tasting menu treats pristine product as the whole point: lobster custard with raspberry butter and a poached claw, a quail egg cured in black walnut miso, caramelized butternut squash with sikil pak. Named No. 1 on North America's 50 Best in 2026, it pairs with the couple's more casual downstairs sibling, The Loyalist.

singlethread-healdsburg-ca.text: SingleThread is a farm, restaurant and five-room inn woven into one experience by chef Kyle Connaughton and farmer Katina Connaughton in downtown Healdsburg. A 24-acre Dry Creek Valley farm supplies the vegetables, fruit, herbs and honey behind a ten-course, kaiseki-influenced menu shaped by the couple's years in Japan — an opening "botanical landscape" of first bites, precise knife work, and the signature donabe clay pot that transforms seafood and vegetables. Inn guests can trade the tasting menu for a family-style donabe hot-pot dinner served in their room.

providence-los-angeles-ca.text: Open since 2005, Michael Cimarusti's Providence is Los Angeles's temple to sustainable seafood — one of the first two restaurants in Greater LA to reach three Michelin stars, and holder of a Green Star for its sourcing. Cimarusti treats pristine, often wild-caught fish with classical French finesse across contemporary tasting menus; the signature is Santa Barbara uni set over a decadent egg yolk, alongside a celebrated caviar service. It is among the most decorated kitchens in the country, and a standard-bearer for the chef-as-conservationist.

eleven-madison-park-new-york-ny.text: Daniel Humm's Eleven Madison Park overlooks its namesake Manhattan park from a grand Art Deco room, and in 2021 it made history as the first entirely plant-based restaurant to hold three Michelin stars. Humm rebuilt the menu around vegetables and invention — a crisp vegan roll with fermented sunflower "butter," a tonburi quenelle mimicking caviar with horseradish cream — keeping its stars along the way. The kitchen has more recently begun reintroducing meat and duck options alongside the plant-based tasting. It remains one of New York's defining fine-dining destinations.

jungsik-new-york-new-york-ny.text: Opened in Tribeca in 2011 by Seoul-born chef Jungsik Yim, Jungsik pioneered a "New Korean" fine dining and, in 2024, became the first Korean restaurant in the United States to earn three Michelin stars — New York's first new three-star in twelve years. A single elegant tasting menu (from about $295, under executive chef Daeik Kim) reinterprets Korean flavors with precision: raw striped jack with white kimchi and chilled fish-bone broth, crisp octopus with gochujang aioli, dry-aged Arctic char in kimchi and red curry. It laid the groundwork for Korean fine dining's rise in America.

per-se-new-york-ny.text: Thomas Keller's New York counterpart to The French Laundry, Per Se has held three Michelin stars since the city's first guide in 2006, perched above Columbus Circle with sweeping Central Park views. Built on the French Laundry's foundation — Keller closed the Yountville flagship for five months to train the team — it serves a daily nine-course tasting, plus a nine-course vegetable menu, of classic French technique and impeccable product. The meal opens, as ever, with "Oysters and Pearls," a sabayon of tapioca pearls with poached oysters and caviar.

sushi-sho-new-york-ny.text: Sushi Sho brought master Keiji Nakazawa's revered Edomae omakase to Midtown Manhattan in 2024, and within a year it became the only sushi restaurant in the U.S. to hold three Michelin stars. Nakazawa — who ran the original Sushi Sho in Tokyo's Yotsuya for more than thirty years — champions the 19th-century Edomae style, curing, simmering and marinating fish rather than serving it merely raw to coax out deeper flavor. The result is a traditional, deeply expressive counter experience rooted in the very origins of sushi.

atelier-crenn-san-francisco-ca.text: At Atelier Crenn, Dominique Crenn became the first female chef in the U.S. to earn three Michelin stars, in 2018. Her deeply personal "poetic culinaria" — the menu has famously read as a poem — traces a journey from her seaside childhood in Brittany to the Pacific, built on pescatarian and plant courses with much of the produce grown at her own Bleu Belle Farm in Sonoma. Seafood, delicate sauces and farm vegetables meet in cooking that is at once indulgent and nourishing, and unmistakably autobiographical.

californios-san-francisco-ca.text: Val Cantú's Californios began as a pop-up and, in 2026, became the first Mexican restaurant in the world to earn three Michelin stars. From its SoMa home the kitchen sends out a roughly 16-course, ~$375 tasting rooted in Cantú's family traditions and his grandmother's cooking, using sustainable ingredients from small California farms — uni-caviar sopes, a matsukasa-yaki fish taco, rack of lamb with mole amarillo and morels. Michelin praised its precision and clarity "without losing the Mexican identity," a landmark for Mexican fine dining.

quince-san-francisco-ca.text: Opened in 2003 by Michael and Lindsay Tusk and in Jackson Square since 2009, Quince is a San Francisco institution that climbed to three Michelin stars in 2017. Tusk's Californian cooking runs on Italian and French technique and Northern California produce, with handmade pasta a perennial highlight — agnolotti of white asparagus, first-of-season peas in a guanciale-and-clam broth. Refined and quietly luxurious, it anchors the Tusks' family of restaurants alongside Cotogna and Verjus.

enclos-sonoma-ca.text: Enclos opened in Sonoma in December 2024 and rose meteorically — two Michelin stars in 2025, three in 2026. Chef Brian Limoges reworks memories of his New Hampshire upbringing into refined eight-to-ten-course tasting menus — a lobster-roll croustade, clam-chowder chawanmushi — built on produce from Stone Edge Farm's carbon-negative estate gardens. The kitchen's regenerative ethos runs deep, even repurposing fallen trees into chopsticks and serving trays, blending California bounty with New England nostalgia.

somni-west-hollywood-ca.text: Somni — Catalan for "dream" — is Aitor Zabala's intimate counter in West Hollywood, and in 2025 it became the first restaurant in Greater Los Angeles to earn three Michelin stars. Zabala, who apprenticed under José Andrés in Barcelona, sends a long, endlessly creative procession of small bites across a contemporary Spanish menu shaped by California: mussel escabeche, gazpacho, an iconic shiso-tartare tempura. Reopened in 2024 after its original Beverly Hills location closed during the pandemic, its handful of seats are among the hardest to get in LA.

alinea-chicago-il.text: Grant Achatz and Nick Kokonas's Alinea is American avant-garde dining at its most theatrical — a maximalist, modernist experience of scented vapors, hidden ingredients and tableside surprise. Long a three-star fixture (2011–2024) before settling at two, it remains one of Chicago's most immersive tables: "pearls" of spiced orange, an edible green-apple-and-helium balloon, and a finale painted directly onto the tabletop as an edible canvas. Whimsy and precision in equal measure, it helped define the genre.

ever-chicago-il.text: Curtis Duffy and partner Michael Muser's Ever occupies a sleek, futuristic Fulton Market room — familiar to viewers of The Bear — where Duffy's ingredient-led cooking turns technical precision into quiet drama. Choose the 12- or 15-course menu, one seafood-and-protein and one vegetable-forward: Ora King salmon with fennel, a tom kha gai hidden under crisped rice and fried chicken skin with fragrant coconut broth poured tableside, wagyu with braised pistachio. It is refined, modern American cooking with a designer's eye for presentation.

oriole-chicago-il.text: Reached through a converted freight elevator in a covert West Loop alley, Oriole is Noah Sandoval's tasting-menu-only hideaway — a former warehouse with a striking ceiling collage over its spotless open kitchen. The long menu blends French and Japanese sensibilities and opens with a luxe salvo of finger food: scallop, jamón ibérico, sea urchin, prawn and caviar. Foie gras with California fig and a restrained black-truffle capellini show a kitchen equally capable of opulence and self-control.

aska-brooklyn-ny.text: Aska — Swedish for "ashes" — is Stockholm-born Fredrik Berselius's New Nordic table in Brooklyn, grown from his earlier pop-up Frej into a two-star destination. Around an open kitchen, a small team sends out a 12-to-16-course menu rooted in foraging, preservation, smoke and seasonality: langoustine with violets, a potato pancake with roe emulsion, and the signature mushroom-fudge-filled æbleskiver with woodruff syrup. Wild herbs, berries and pristine seafood give the meal a Nordic soul without dogma.

atomix-new-york-ny.text: Junghyun "JP" Park and his wife and partner Ellia built Atomix into one of the world's most acclaimed Korean restaurants — No. 6 on the World's 50 Best in 2024, the highest-ranked U.S. restaurant that year. Just twelve seats ring a U-shaped counter in NoMad, where a ten-course "New Korean" menu arrives with collectible ceramics and illustrated cards: gim seaweed rice cake with trout roe and perilla, galbi with fermented soybean, Jeju abalone with watermelon. Everything, from the word "Ato" (gift) to the interiors, is crafted by Korean makers.

jean-georges-new-york-ny.text: Since 1997, Jean-Georges Vongerichten's flagship overlooking Columbus Circle has served the lighter, brighter French cooking that made his name — stocks and cream traded for herbal vinaigrettes and vegetable-forward plates with Asian accents. Two Michelin stars and a longtime four-star New York Times rating attest to its staying power. Signatures endure: egg toast with caviar, foie gras with sour-cherry granola, and tuna ribbons that have been on the menu for more than two decades, capped by his famous molten chocolate cake.

masa-new-york-ny.text: Masayoshi Takayama's Masa is New York's most expensive restaurant, an austere Columbus Circle sanctuary built around a $260,000 slab of hinoki cypress and fish flown in daily from Japan. First in the U.S. to hold three Michelin stars for sushi — a title it kept fifteen years before moving to two in 2025 — it remains a singular omakase of foie gras nigiri, Masa toro crowned with osetra caviar, and otherworldly abalone. Seatings run from $750 to a $1,200 seasonal omakase; there is no menu, only Masa.

chef-s-table-at-brooklyn-fare-new-york-n.text: Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare began beside a Brooklyn grocery store and became the first NYC restaurant outside Manhattan to earn three Michelin stars, later moving to a counter in Hell's Kitchen. After founding chef César Ramirez departed in 2023, owner Moe Issa reopened it under co-executive chefs Max Natmessnig and Marco Prins, and Michelin re-awarded two stars. The format holds: an intimate counter and a seafood-forward, seasonal tasting menu served to just a handful of guests.

gabriel-kreuther-new-york-ny.text: Across from Bryant Park in Midtown, Gabriel Kreuther brings the Alsatian-born chef's homeland to a polished two-star dining room marked by his signature stork motif. Kreuther's cooking is rooted in classic French technique with an Alsatian heart — a warm kugelhopf with chive fromage blanc, a smoked-sturgeon-and-sauerkraut tart, and foie gras in myriad guises, seared with quince and chestnut or tucked beside squab. An old-school cheese trolley and a deep list of Alsatian wines complete the ritual.

saison-san-francisco-ca.text: At Saison, in San Francisco's SoMa, seasonal California ingredients meet smoke and flame across an open wood-fire kitchen. Executive chef Richard Lee builds intimate, live-fire tasting menus, roughly $328 to $500-plus, around vegetables, seafood and meats kissed by the hearth, served to a small room with a six-seat bar and a private kitchen table for those who want to sit closest to the fire. It is an elemental, ingredient-driven expression of Northern California.

blue-hill-at-stone-barns-tarrytown-ny.text: On a working farm in the Hudson Valley, Dan Barber's Blue Hill at Stone Barns turns agriculture into dinner — a two-star, Green-Star kitchen whose sprawling multi-course menu changes daily, even table to table, by whatever the fields and greenhouses offer that morning. Barber has gone so far as to breed vegetables to order, like his heatless Habanada pepper. Less a meal than an edible snapshot of the surrounding farm, it is among the most influential farm-to-table restaurants in America.

the-inn-at-little-washington-washington-.text: Patrick O'Connell opened The Inn at Little Washington in a Virginia crossroads in 1978, determined to bring world-class dining to the American countryside — teaching himself from Julia Child and making pilgrimages to France's great restaurants for a benchmark. Decades on, it is among the most celebrated country inns in the world, serving a regional American cuisine built on local farms and the Inn's own garden. Its menus range from enduring classics — herb-crusted Elysian Fields lamb carpaccio with Caesar-salad ice cream — to butter-poached Maine lobster and a fully vegetarian tasting.

aubergine-carmel-by-the-sea-ca.text: Inside L'Auberge Carmel, Aubergine is Carmel-by-the-Sea's most decorated dining room, where former professional figure skater turned chef Justin Cogley builds an eight-course tasting around Monterey Bay's bounty in an intimate nine-table space. The menu changes daily — a "cabbage" taco of shallot jam, braised treviso and Kaluga caviar; a Dungeness crab rice roulade in white dashi; triple-seared dry-aged ribeye brushed with wagyu XO. Classic technique meets a sleek, modern sense of place on the Monterey coast.

vespertine-culver-city-ca.text: Jordan Kahn's Vespertine is less a restaurant than an immersive art piece, set inside a futuristic red-steel building — nicknamed "The Waffle" — in Culver City, where diners move between floors as the meal unfolds. Reopened in 2024 after a four-year pandemic closure, and awarded both two Michelin stars and a Green Star, it serves a daringly inventive, at times whimsical tasting: scallop with passionfruit and ají amarillo under a horseradish tuile, an "obsidian mirror" of smoked mussel cream with salted plum. Sculptural, otherworldly and singular.

kato-los-angeles-ca.text: Jon Yao's Kato began in a West LA strip mall in 2016 and, after moving to a larger Arts District home in 2022, became one of Los Angeles's most admired tasting-menu tables, earning its first Michelin star in 2019. Yao reinterprets the Taiwanese and Chinese flavors of his mother's cooking through a Southern California lens: a yóutiáo doughnut filled with sea urchin and brown-butter emulsion under jamón and caviar; fish maw with Dungeness crab and custard; spice-crusted duck with a fluffy bao. Personal, precise and quietly ambitious.

hayato-los-angeles-ca.text: Brandon Go spent two decades studying traditional Japanese technique, much of it in three-star kitchens in Japan, before opening Hayato in Downtown LA's Arts District in 2018 — his vision of a chef-owned, authentic kaiseki restaurant. At a seven-seat counter he sends out a deeply personal, season-driven kaiseki, each ingredient sliced, grilled, fried or steamed to exacting standards and explained in detail. It earned its first Michelin star in 2019 and a second in 2021, an intimate temple to Japanese precision.

aquavit-new-york-ny.text: Open since 1987, Aquavit introduced New York to Scandinavian fine dining, and under executive chef Emma Bengtsson — the first Swedish woman to earn two Michelin stars — it remains the city's benchmark for Nordic cooking. A former pastry chef, Bengtsson brings precision to tasting menus of pristine seafood, cultured dairy and preserved, seasonal produce: Norwegian langoustine with Meyer-lemon sabayon, halibut with salt-baked celeriac and smoked-whey beurre blanc. Elegant desserts thread citrus, herb and licorice notes through a distinctly Swedish sensibility.

atera-new-york-ny.text: In a spare Tribeca room, Danish chef Ronny Emborg's Atera seats just a dozen guests around an open-kitchen counter for a roughly 20-course tasting of Nordic-inflected, globally curious cooking — some herbs grown in a hidden sub-basement garden. The all-inclusive menu carries no surcharge even for caviar or truffle: a lobster taco with caviar, a fried cheese ball shaved with fresh truffle, trout roe and foie gras wrapped in crisp nori. Minimalist plating, maximal luxury.

saga-new-york-ny.text: Perched on the 63rd floor of the Art Deco tower at 70 Pine Street, Saga wraps a two-star tasting menu in 360-degree Financial District views, across a multi-floor space with a solarium and outdoor terraces. Founded in 2021 by acclaimed chef James Kent — an Eleven Madison Park veteran — and carried on by its kitchen team after his untimely death, it serves American cooking with a continental European hand, from a modern Lobster Newberg to a composed Duck à la Royale. As much a skyline experience as a meal.

the-modern-new-york-ny.text: At the foot of MoMA, overlooking the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, The Modern pairs museum-grade surroundings with Thomas Allan's contemporary American cooking and its French accents. The two-star dining room turns out refined, quietly playful, ingredient-led plates — honeynut squash with razor clams, dry-aged duck with red endive and quince, a brûléed bread pudding — while the adjacent Bar Room offers a more casual à la carte. It is part of Danny Meyer's Union Square Hospitality Group.

sushi-noz-new-york-ny.text: On the Upper East Side, Hokkaido-born Nozomu Abe presides over Sushi Noz, an Edomae omakase counter built from more than a thousand pieces of Japanese cedar assembled without a single nail, centered on a 200-year-old hinoki bar. Two intimate rooms seat just fourteen guests total for a meticulous, many-course tasting; Abe, who trained under Edomae masters in Tokyo, draws on a childhood around his grandfather's seafood company. Elevated to two Michelin stars in 2023, it is among New York's purest sushi experiences.

melisse-santa-monica-ca.text: A Santa Monica institution since 1999, Josiah Citrin's Mélisse was reborn as an intimate fourteen-seat room where Citrin and chef-partner Ken Takayama guide a lavish, roughly two-and-a-half-hour French tasting. Entered through a discreet side door, it trades in unabashed decadence — Santa Barbara uni, A5 wagyu, Royal Osetra caviar, generous tableside saucing — and closes with a signature dry-aged duck "Rouennaise" finished on an antique silver press. Two-star, old-world luxury filtered through California ingredients.

jont-washington-dc.text: Tucked behind its sister restaurant in DC's 14th Street corridor, Jônt is Ryan Ratino's sixteen-seat counter marrying Japanese precision and seasonality to French luxury and live-fire cooking. The fifteen-course tasting is built on some of the world's rarest ingredients — wagyu and foie gras, Kaluga caviar, Miyazaki mango — in dishes like a wagyu-tartare tart, Hokkaido uni crowned with bluefin, and Koshiibuki rice with Dungeness crab, maitake and shaved Australian black truffle. Ratino won the Michelin Guide's DC Young Chef Award in 2023.

minibar-by-jose-andres-washington-dc.text: minibar is José Andrés's avant-garde flagship — his first U.S. fine-dining venture, opened in 2003 and now a twelve-seat chef's counter in DC's Penn Quarter behind a discreet corner sign. The two-star tasting is a study in culinary science and theater, each bite engineered to surprise as it blends tradition with technique. Reservations, released at noon on the first of each month, routinely vanish within a day; a private José's Table sits beside the kitchen for a party of up to six.

the-wolf-s-tailor-denver-co.text: Kelly Whitaker's The Wolf's Tailor made history as Colorado's first two-Michelin-star restaurant — a first star in 2023, a second in 2025 — and holds a Green Star to match. In a Sunnyside space built around a binchotan grill, wood-fired oven, house fermentation program and mill for heritage grains, Whitaker's "In Defense of the Maker" ethos honors the farmers, millers and craftspeople behind each course. Global influences ground local ingredients: an all-corn caviar service with cream and blini made from corn, robata-grilled bison with chile-peach and dan dan noodles, spring lamb with rhubarb tonkatsu.

harbor-house-inn-elk-ca.text: On a wild stretch of Mendocino coast three hours north of San Francisco, the Harbor House Inn pairs a ten-room retreat with a twenty-seat, two-star dining room led by chef Matthew Kammerer. His strictly sustainable, hyper-local cooking — also a Green Star holder — draws on seafood, foraged forest ingredients and seaweed harvested from the Inn's own cove, cooked over fire, steam and smoke with reverential Japanese touches. Dungeness crab, sea urchin and even lace lichen become quiet luxuries in one of California's most remote fine-dining destinations.

l-atelier-de-joel-robuchon-miami-miami-f.text: In Miami's Design District, L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon carries the late master's signature format — a red-and-black counter wrapped around an open kitchen, rosewood and leather, guests facing the chefs at a 34-seat bar. Florida's only two-Michelin-star restaurant and the sole two-star Robuchon in the U.S., it serves modern French cooking à la carte or by tasting menu: seared scallops in cilantro broth with coconut foam, lamb with eggplant caponata in fairytale-eggplant cups. Precise, luxurious and unmistakably Robuchon.

emeril-s-new-orleans-la.text: Emeril Lagasse's 1990 New Orleans flagship has been reborn as a two-star tasting-menu destination — the only restaurant in the American South to hold two Michelin stars — now led by his son E.J. Lagasse. The reimagined seven-course menu, closer to a dozen bites over three-plus hours at around $295, celebrates bold Creole flavors with meticulous technique: foie gras in a silky oyster stew flecked with herb oil, boudin humming with Creole spice. A legacy restaurant remade for a new generation.

cesar-new-york-ny.text: After more than a decade earning three Michelin stars at Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare, César Ramirez opened his eponymous César in SoHo in 2023 — and earned two Michelin stars within five months. Still at the stoves nightly, the self-taught chef builds a twelve-course tasting around world-class seafood shipped from everywhere, filtered through French and Japanese sensibilities in an understated, century-old space. It climbed to No. 10 on North America's 50 Best in 2026.

joo-ok-new-york-ny.text: Joo Ok earned two Michelin stars in Seoul, then relocated to New York's Koreatown in 2024 — and won two stars again within a year. Reached by freight elevator sixteen stories up, chef Chang-ho Shin's serene, skyline-view room echoes a traditional Korean home for a twelve-course, $270 tasting built on seasonality, fermentation and a house pantry of jang. Dishes like makgeolli bread with seared sea bass and a pheasant-and-foie-gras mandu explore Korean royal cuisine through American-grown ingredients.

odo-new-york-ny.text: Hidden behind a door at the back of a Flatiron cocktail bar, Odo is Hiroki Odo's thirteen-seat kaiseki counter — a rustic-minimalist room where the Kyushu-born chef, who trained for a decade in Kyoto, Nagoya and Tokyo and later led the acclaimed Kajitsu, cooks by the customs of traditional kaiseki. The eight-course menu hinges on peak-season ingredients from local fishermen and farmers and from Japan. It earned a star in its first year of eligibility and rose to two in 2023.

commis-oakland-ca.text: On Oakland's Piedmont Avenue, James Syhabout's Commis was the East Bay's first Michelin-starred restaurant and remains its most decorated at two stars. Syhabout pairs precise technique with his Thai and Chinese heritage across a ten-course, roughly $279 tasting that bridges East and West: raw Japanese sea bream with aged soy, fermented plum and mustard; a signature slow-poached egg yolk in onion-malt cream; donabe-baked scallion rice with chanterelles. Serene, warm and quietly virtuosic.

sorekara-orlando-fl.text: In Orlando's Baldwin Park, William Shen's Sorekara became just the second restaurant in Florida to earn two Michelin stars — a high-concept, one-seating-a-night experience that moves through multiple rooms over several hours. Shen's 20-plus-course tasting is organized around Japan's 72 micro-seasons and threaded with whimsy, including a course that riffs on a convenience-store snack run, alongside pristine madai and Hokkaido kegani crab. Photos are gently discouraged; the point is to be present.

acquerello-san-francisco-ca.text: Since 1989, Acquerello has set San Francisco's standard for classic Italian fine dining, with chef and co-owner Suzette Gresham cooking in a converted chapel on Sacramento Street. Her two-star, prix-fixe menu balances tradition and refinement — handmade pastas like rabbit marubini in prosciutto brodo, Liberty duck cured under red-wine pomace, a Swiss-chard-and-mushroom raviolo — and ends with one of the city's great mignardise carts, stacked with chocolates, pâtes de fruits and caramels. Simple elegance, perfected over decades.

birdsong-san-francisco-ca.text: In SoMa, Chris Bleidorn's Birdsong turns live fire into two-star cooking, drawing on his time at Alinea, Benu, Atelier Crenn and Saison to honor heritage foodways through smoke, cure and open flame. The three-hour "Journey" tasting balances the rugged and the delicate: lacquered quail with grilled Parker House rolls to assemble Peking-duck style, creek trout "roe" with kelp-kombucha sabayon, sweet-and-salty cornbread with grilled walnut butter and caviar. Fire-driven and deeply Californian.

kiln-san-francisco-ca.text: Opened in 2023 in Hayes Valley by chef John Wesley and general manager Julianna Yang, Kiln builds a two-star tasting on preservation — curing, drying, fermentation and pickling — across an 18-to-20-course, largely Nordic progression of dishes that often take days to prepare. Simplicity masks intricate technique: a crispy curlicue of puffed beef tendon among the opening snacks, a squab breast lacquered in burnt honey with a truffled jus. Quiet, warehouse-set and technically exacting.

lazy-bear-san-francisco-ca.text: Lazy Bear began in 2009 as an underground supper club in David Barzelay's apartment — thrown by a laid-off lawyer whose dinner parties became a career — and grew into a two-Michelin-star Mission District "dinner party" unlike anything else in San Francisco. Guests gather communally for an evolving tasting that reads as a seasonal map of the Bay Area, blending local ingredients, inventive technique and a streak of American nostalgia. It won a star in its first eligible year and two the next.

sons-and-daughters-san-francisco-ca.text: Sons & Daughters is San Francisco's New Nordic outlier, a two-star and Green Star room where chef Harrison Cheney reinterprets Scandinavian traditions through Bay Area seasonality since taking over in 2023. The ambitious 24-course, $315 tasting leans on foraging and fermentation: rutabaga "noodles" in pork fat and sabayon, a quail-sausage Scotch egg with a molten quail yolk, knäckebröd with smoked whitefish roe, Mt. Lassen trout with dill vinegar and currant-wood oil. Deliberately calibrated toward a third star.

63-clinton-new-york-ny.text: On a quiet Lower East Side corner, 63 Clinton is chef Sam Clonts and partner Raymond Trinh's warm rewrite of fine-dining convention — Clonts trained five-plus years at Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare before opening here in 2021 and winning a Michelin star within months. The seasonal tasting draws on the pair's Southeastern Arizona upbringing and Sonoran flavors, plus thoughtful whole-animal butchery: a breakfast-taco opener, smoked corn with razor clams and caviar, Berkshire pork short rib with shishito, a strawberry-yuzu baked Alaska. Approachable, precise and personal.

bar-miller-new-york-ny.text: Bar Miller is an eight-seat East Village jewel box from the sustainability-minded Ume Hospitality team behind Rosella next door — a Michelin-starred omakase that flips the luxury-sushi script. Rather than rare fish flown in daily, its roughly fifteen-course menu sources almost entirely from U.S. waters, making Massachusetts mackerel feel as luxurious as a Hokkaido scallop while avoiding overfished species. The tiny room centers on a striking L-shaped counter of blue-green Avocatus quartzite, framed by oak and burl. Thoughtful, local and quietly radical.

bridges-new-york-ny.text: In a warm, amber-lit room on Chinatown's Chatham Square, Bridges is Australian chef Sam Lawrence's ambitious take on European bistro cooking — French and Basque traditions filtered through a New York sensibility. An Estela alumnus, Lawrence opened in 2024 and earned a Michelin star by late 2025 with a tight, hard-to-categorize menu: cured tuna with black trumpet and dates, a Comté-custard tart with morels, grilled king crab, roast duck, a vin jaune gelato. Convivial ease meets serious drive.

bom-new-york-ny.text: Tucked behind its sister restaurant Oiji Mi in the Flatiron — "bōm" means spring, and also "Back of Oiji Mi" — this seventeen-seat counter is Brian Kim's opulent contemporary Korean tasting, Michelin-starred since its 2023 debut. Guests ring a U-shaped marble counter with built-in grills as luxury piles on luxury: prime wagyu, uni, caviar and truffle threaded through course after course, traditional Korean flavors met with modern technique. Intimate, indulgent and theatrical.

cafe-boulud-new-york-ny.text: Daniel Boulud's more relaxed Upper East Side room, Café Boulud organizes its cooking around the chef's four muses — La Tradition (classic French), La Saison (the seasons), Le Potager (the garden) and Le Voyage (world flavors). In a polished Art Deco-inspired dining room, executive chef Romain Paumier builds on classical French foundations with seasonal and global touches: a signature potato-wrapped black sea bass in red-wine sauce, an impeccable tarte Tatin. Elegant, versatile and quintessentially Boulud.

casa-mono-new-york-ny.text: A tiny, buzzing tapas bar near Gramercy's Irving Place, Casa Mono has held a Michelin star every year since 2009 — a rare feat for a room this casual. Opened in 2003 by Mario Batali, Joe Bastianich and chef Andy Nusser and inspired by Spain's Costa Brava, it leans into bold, protein-forward small plates: razor clams a la plancha, confit goat, creamy eggs with sea urchin and anchovy oil, octopus with asparagus. Its sibling wine-and-ham bar, Bar Jamón, sits next door.

corima-new-york-ny.text: On the Lower East Side–Chinatown border, Corima is Fidel Caballero's "progressive Mexican" — northern-Mexico cooking, drawn from a Ciudad Juárez and El Paso childhood, filtered through his time at three-star Martín Berasategui and NYC's Contra. Michelin-starred since its 2024 opening, the globe-trotting menu roams from tlayudas and tetelas to katsu sandos and tamales: a smoked-swordfish tamal, potato udon in cornhusk dashi, chocolate flan. Bon Appétit named it a best new restaurant, and it cracked North America's 50 Best.

cote-new-york-ny.text: Simon Kim's Cote fuses Korean barbecue with the American steakhouse — a Flatiron "Korean Steakhouse" that earned a Michelin star within a year of its 2017 opening, the first of its kind to do so. Smokeless live-fire grills sit in every table for guests to cook dry-aged USDA Prime and American wagyu themselves, amid banchan and kimchi, with executive chef David Shim in the kitchen and a serious wine list alongside. Cote runs the only in-house dry-aging room of any Korean steakhouse in New York.

crown-shy-new-york-ny.text: On the ground floor of the landmark Art Deco tower at 70 Pine Street, Crown Shy was the late chef James Kent's first solo project, with partner Jeff Katz, and it won a Michelin star just six months after opening in 2019 — a distinction it has held since. Under soaring ceilings and marble, the globally curious, European-rooted menu leans convivial: pull-apart olive bread, gruyère fritters, mafaldine with rock shrimp and chorizo, ras-el-hanout short rib, sticky toffee pudding. The more relaxed counterpart to Kent's Saga upstairs.

daniel-new-york-ny.text: For more than three decades, Daniel Boulud's flagship has been the Upper East Side's grand stage for French fine dining — a Bernardaud-chandeliered, Rosenquist-hung room built for special occasions and brokered deals. Boulud's credo, the finest American produce by French tradition, plays out in seasonal menus: Castroville artichoke ravioli in barigoule consommé, ikejime black cod with cauliflower cream and beluga lentils, a Blue Ridge rabbit duo with morels. Iconic, formal and enduring.

dirt-candy-new-york-ny.text: Amanda Cohen's Dirt Candy pioneered New York's vegetable-forward movement — the city's first vegetable-focused restaurant when it opened in a tiny East Village space in 2008, now a Lower East Side room and one of only two vegetarian restaurants in NYC to hold a Michelin star. Cohen, not a vegetarian herself, treats produce as "candy from the earth," spinning single vegetables into inventive, playful courses. It was also an early mover on eliminating tipping and sharing profits with staff.

essential-by-christophe-new-york-ny.text: On the Upper West Side near Lincoln Center, Essential by Christophe is chef Christophe Bellanca's pared-back vision of modern French cooking — "only the essentials." Ardèche-raised and trained in a who's-who of French kitchens, including six years with Anne-Sophie Pic at Maison Pic, before leading Le Cirque and Robuchon's U.S. ateliers, Bellanca opened here in 2022 and earned a Michelin star in 2023. The refined, ingredient-driven tasting menus pair classic technique with restraint and subtle global accents.

estela-new-york-ny.text: A floor above East Houston Street, Ignacio Mattos's Estela is a bistro at heart that reinvents the familiar — tartare, ricotta dumplings, burrata on toast — into something restrained yet expressive. Since 2013 its shareable American-Mediterranean plates have earned a Michelin star and a spot on the World's 50 Best, built on unexpected combinations that feel both natural and precise. Signatures endure: ricotta dumplings with mushrooms, and the ink-black arroz negro with squid and hazelnuts.

family-meal-at-blue-hill-new-york-ny.text: Dan Barber first opened Blue Hill in Greenwich Village in 2000, four years before his celebrated upstate farm restaurant — and its latest, pandemic-born incarnation, Family Meal, may be its most quietly radical. Named for the staff meal cooks share before service, it serves a single menuless, seasonally driven, vegetable-dominated spread family-style, sourced largely from Blue Hill at Stone Barns. A Green Star restaurant where sustainability and relaxed elegance guide every plate.

francie-brooklyn-ny.text: Set in a former limestone bank building in Williamsburg and named for A Tree Grows in Brooklyn, Francie is Christopher Cipollone's Michelin-starred modern American brasserie — Left Bank warmth of exposed brick, mosaic floors and cozy booths. Cipollone weaves Italian, French and Korean influences through a flexible menu that runs from upscale bar snacks and shellfish to handmade pasta and showpieces like a crown roast of duck and côte de boeuf for two. Convivial and confident.

frevo-new-york-ny.text: Frevo hides a sixteen-seat chef's counter behind a rotating Greenwich Village art gallery — you enter through one of the exhibition's pieces. Brazilian-born chef Franco Sampogna, an alumnus of Guy Savoy and Alain Ducasse, earned a Michelin star in 2022 for a ten-course French tasting centered on the expressive power of sauces, shaded with South American and Asian flavors. Part fine-dining room, part contemporary gallery, it trades on discovery and exclusivity.

gramercy-tavern-new-york-ny.text: A New York institution since 1994, Danny Meyer's Gramercy Tavern pairs a casual, walk-in Tavern with a more formal Dining Room, both anchored by chef-partner Michael Anthony's seasonal New American cooking. Anthony, who took over in 2006, works "by subtraction" — legible dishes, sauces built on depth, vegetables treated as narrative even when they aren't the headline — sustained by deep local-farm relationships. A Michelin star, a three-star Times review and multiple James Beard Awards attest to its enduring standard.

huso-new-york-ny.text: Huso is Top Chef winner Buddha Lo's Michelin-starred tasting-menu room hidden inside Marky's Caviar — first a speakeasy behind the Madison Avenue shop, and since early 2025 an elegant twelve-course space in Tribeca. As its caviar pedigree suggests, the seasonal menu leans luxurious — caviar, white truffle, Champagne — executed with precision and polished hospitality. A Robb Report best-new-restaurant honoree, intimate and indulgent.

icca-new-york-ny.text: Behind a discreet Tribeca facade and a sleek cocktail bar, Icca is chef Kazushige Suzuki's omakase, Michelin-starred within its first year. Suzuki draws prized fish direct from Tokyo's Toyosu market, balancing tradition and invention across signatures like longtooth grouper, black abalone, Hokkaido hairy crab with capellini and shiso, and a snow trout marinated seven days in koji. Understated, immersive and deeply umami.

jeju-noodle-bar-new-york-ny.text: Jeju Noodle Bar is the first — and long the only — noodle restaurant in the U.S. to earn a Michelin star, all the more remarkable since chef Douglas Kim had never cooked a noodle before opening it. A no-frills West Village room, it centers on "ramyun," the Korean take on ramen: handmade noodles in bold, rich broths from wagyu to lobster, dressed with anything from heirloom tomato to white truffle. Non-noodle standouts include the Toro Ssam Bap and a famously crispy fried-chicken platter.

jua-new-york-ny.text: In a loft-like Flatiron room warmed by a wood-burning grill, Jua is Hoyoung Kim's modern Korean tasting built on live fire — a former executive chef of two-star Jungsik, Ferrandi-trained and an L'Astrance alum, who named the restaurant for his firstborn daughter. The seven-course menu balances tradition and refinement: chilled mulhoe in spicy broth, smoked-eel jook, crispy-seaweed tuna tartare, wood-fired galbi, dry-aged fish with crackling skin. Smoke and precision in equal measure.

joji-new-york-ny.text: Tucked into a hidden alcove beneath One Vanderbilt by Grand Central, Jōji is a serene omakase oasis born of a partnership between developer SL Green, chef George Ruan and Daniel Boulud's Dinex Group. Chef-partners George Ruan and Wayne Cheng lead a traditional multi-course omakase for a ten-seat counter and eight-seat private room, tailored to each guest with premium sake and wine. Michelin-starred calm amid the Midtown rush.

kochi-new-york-ny.text: Kochi — Korean for "skewer" — turns royal Joseon-dynasty fare into an inventive, hand-to-mouth tasting in Hell's Kitchen, Michelin-starred for its expertly grilled skewers and bold compositions. Opened in 2019 by chefs Sungchul Shim and Byeong Seok Lee, its eight-course menu, with an optional abalone add-on, runs from beet-soup croquettes to octopus skewers, soy-braised abalone and playful banana-tangerine desserts. Personal, engaging and refreshingly unstuffy.

kosaka-new-york-ny.text: On a quiet West Village street, Kosaka is Yoshihiko Kousaka's elegant Edomae sushi room — a Jewel Bako veteran and traditionalist who has held a Michelin star for years. At a twelve-seat counter, with a few tables besides, soft piano accompanies a single omakase of amuse, sashimi and a dozen sushi courses with soup, dessert and tea. Refined, classical and quietly luxurious.

la-bastide-by-andrea-calstier-north-sale.text: An hour north of Manhattan in Westchester's North Salem, La Bastide is a six-table modern-farmhouse room where chef Andrea Calstier and general manager Elena Oliver bring Provence to the Hudson Valley. Marseille-trained and a Daniel Boulud alum, Calstier opened this hyperlocal, multi-course tasting in February 2024 and earned a Michelin star within a year, drawing on his southern-French upbringing and the surrounding pastoral landscape. It shares a roof with the couple's more casual Cenadou Bistrot.

le-coucou-new-york-ny.text: Le Coucou marked chef Daniel Rose's celebrated return to the U.S. in 2016 — a collaboration with restaurateur Stephen Starr that the James Beard Foundation named Best New Restaurant before it took a Michelin star. In a candlelit, Roman-and-Williams-designed room near SoHo, the Chicago-born, France-trained Rose cooks unapologetically classic French with personality: pike quenelles, sautéed sweetbreads with tomato crème, and a theatrical three-act rabbit. Old-school technique, warmly delivered.

le-pavillon-new-york-ny.text: On the second floor of One Vanderbilt, Daniel Boulud's Le Pavillon is a lush, garden-like oasis — olive trees and soaring ceilings above Midtown — devoted to seafood- and vegetable-forward contemporary French cooking. Michelin-starred since its first year in 2022, its menu leans on Northeast fishermen and farmers: spaghetti alla chitarra in Meyer-lemon butter crowned with Kaluga caviar, roasted cauliflower with Aleppo muhammara and heirloom beans. Serene, seasonal and refined.

l-abeille-new-york-ny.text: On a cobblestoned Tribeca corner, L'Abeille — "the bee" in French, echoing chef Mitsunobu Nagae's name (honey in Japanese) — filters French bistronomy through a Japanese sensibility. Nagae trained in Lyon and cooked in three-star kitchens in France, Tokyo and New York, including Robuchon's ateliers, before opening here in 2022 and earning a Michelin star. His prix-fixe menus lighten French classics: a California squab with miso and a mole-inspired chocolate-bourbon sauce, grilled trout with Champagne-caviar sauce, lychee mousse with strawberry and shiso.

mari-new-york-ny.text: Mari — "roll" in Korean — is Sungchul Shim's second Michelin-starred Hell's Kitchen restaurant, after Kochi, a tasting menu built around elevated Korean hand rolls inspired by street food. Shim, a Culinary Institute of America grad who cooked at Le Bernardin, Per Se and Aureole, pairs the rolls with an extensive wine list and Korean spirits like soju and makgeolli. Opened in 2021 and starred within a year, it is a creative, precise evolution of Korean-American cooking.

meju-queens-ny.text: Meju is an eight-seat counter hidden behind the Little Banchan Shop in Long Island City — Queens' only Michelin-starred restaurant — where chef Hooni Kim builds a deeply personal menu around jang, the traditional Korean seasoning pastes he has wild-fermented and aged for a decade. Named for the dried soybean blocks that start fermentation, its multi-course tasting showcases doenjang, gochujang and ganjang with silky tofu, fried pancakes, Miyazaki beef and Niman Ranch pork, served on handmade Korean clay and closing, humbly, with rice and kimchi.

muku-new-york-ny.text: Muku made New York history in 2025, earning a Michelin star just two months after opening — the city's fastest ever. In a ten-seat Tribeca counter, the former Sushi Ichimura space, chef Manabu Asanuma builds a kaiseki-inspired menu around goho, the "rule of five" techniques — raw, grilled, simmered, steamed and fried — with rigorous seasonality: wagyu shabu-shabu, gohan with chicken and maitake, soba from the chef's hometown buckwheat. Simple, intentional and masterful.

noda-new-york-ny.text: Noda is an intimate eight-seat Flatiron omakase where Tokyo-born chef Shigeyuki Tsunoda — a Sushi Iwa veteran — pairs traditional Edomae technique with a warmer, more social and opulent setting. Michelin-starred since 2020, the roughly twenty-course seasonal menu moves from small snacks to pristine nigiri like sea eel and two kinds of uni, served over a half-moon cypress counter fronted by the team's speakeasy cocktail den, Shinji. Traditional sushi, modern mood.

noz-17-new-york-ny.text: Noz 17 is Nozomu Abe's more experimental, more accessible companion to his two-star Sushi Noz — a seven-seat cypress counter on a quiet Chelsea side street, led by head chef Junichi Matsuzaki, Abe's longtime second. The Michelin-starred, Edomae-style omakase runs to some thirty courses in a serene, wood-lined room, with a shorter fifteen-course bar menu offering the same quality for less. A calm, considered sushi sanctuary.

noksu-new-york-ny.text: Nōksu hides a fifteen-seat black-marble counter twenty feet underground, behind a code-locked door inside the Herald Square subway entrance in Koreatown — one of New York's most improbable fine-dining rooms. Chef Dae Kim, Per Se-trained and still in his late twenties, sends out a nine-course tasting that filters Korean flavors through French and Japanese technique, seafood-forward with crab, fluke and mackerel and a signature dry-aged squab. The New York Times called it "uncannily good."

oiji-mi-new-york-ny.text: In a sleek Flatiron dining room, Brian Kim's Oiji Mi reimagines the prix-fixe as polished modern Korean — elegant, restrained and Michelin-starred just five months after its 2022 opening. Kim, a CIA grad who cooked at the two-star Bouley and runs the original Oiji, favors refinement over boldness: beef tartare with celeriac and caviar, seared scallop with mustard-leaf kimchi and miyeok-guk foam, chilled lobster ramyun. Its higher-end sibling, bōm, hides at the back.

oxomoco-brooklyn-ny.text: Oxomoco brings wood-fired Mexican cooking to a sunlit, plant-filled Greenpoint room — from the Speedy Romeo team, built around an open live-fire kitchen and led by chef Justin Bazdarich. Michelin-starred and deceptively casual, it centers on tacos piled with chanterelles, lamb barbacoa, masa-tempura shrimp or the day's catch, alongside a tropical hamachi aguachile, a smoky-corn tlayuda, best-in-class guacamole and a grilled pollo a las brasas. Serious cooking in a resort-like setting.

restaurant-yuu-brooklyn-ny.text: At an eighteen-seat Greenpoint counter, Restaurant Yuu is chef Yuu Shimano's marriage of classic French technique and Japanese omotenashi. Osaka's Tsuji Institute-trained and a veteran of Guy Savoy in Paris, Shimano opens each service with a theatrical flourish — curtains drawn back to reveal the full kitchen brigade — before an eighteen-course tasting of eel-and-foie-gras risotto, Petrossian-caviar brioche, Arctic char with abalone risotto and a truffle-shaved canard. Michelin-starred since 2023, beauty and boldness on every plate.

rezdora-new-york-ny.text: Rezdôra — dialect for the nonna who hand-rolls the family's pasta — is Stefano Secchi's love letter to Emilia-Romagna in the Flatiron. Secchi honed his craft under Massimo Bottura at three-star Osteria Francescana, and it shows in playful, Bottura-esque dishes like "Grandma Walking Through the Forest," cappelletti verdi with leeks and black-mushroom purée, alongside gnocco fritto and rotating handmade pastas. Michelin-starred since 2021, it channels Northern Italy through a single obsessive lens: pasta.

semma-new-york-ny.text: Semma is the only Indian restaurant in America to hold a Michelin star — a bold, uncompromising expression of Tamil Nadu's cooking from chef Vijay Kumar and the Unapologetic Foods group. In a Greenwich Village room, Kumar, a 2025 James Beard Best Chef: New York State winner, serves the Chettinad and micro-regional dishes of his childhood without softening them for American palates, from gunpowder-dusted classics to snail curry and goat intestine. Rooted, fearless and deeply personal.

shmone-new-york-ny.text: Shmoné — Hebrew for "eight" — is celebrated Israeli chef Eyal Shani's Greenwich Village room, with the kitchen led by principal chef Nadav Greenberg and a Michelin star since 2023. Its "Neo-Levantine" cooking is pure intuition and market-driven seasonality: menus shift as spring vegetables arrive or the day's catch dictates, spanning a sabich plate, chicken kebab and a yogurt-and-sumac dessert. Contemporary Middle Eastern cooking built on exceptional, ever-changing produce.

shota-omakase-brooklyn-ny.text: Named for the sushi manga Shōta no Sushi, Shota Omakase is chef-owner Cheng Lin's Williamsburg counter, Michelin-starred within a year of its 2023 opening. Lin — who trained at Hatsuhana, Sushi Seki and alongside Masa's team at ITO — builds an ever-changing eighteen-course Edomae omakase on marinating, curing and aging: four small plates, soup, eleven seasonal nigiri, a hand roll and a layered tamago finish. Traditional craft meets daily-changing invention.

sushi-nakazawa-new-york-new-york-ny.text: Sushi Nakazawa is the West Village omakase of Daisuke Nakazawa — the apprentice made famous by Jiro Dreams of Sushi, who trained years under Jiro Ono. At a sleek ten-seat counter, his roughly twenty-course sushi progression pairs supremely tender fish with warm, seasoned rice, a spark of wasabi and a judicious brush of nikiri: Hokkaido cherry salmon, live Massachusetts scallop, outstanding uni, a fatty-tuna hand roll. Michelin-starred and, at its price, among New York's best omakase values.

tempura-matsui-new-york-ny.text: Tempura Matsui is America's only Michelin-starred restaurant devoted entirely to tempura — a Murray Hill counter that has held its star for a decade. Under chef Kiyoshi Chikano, whose 27 years of frying build on founder Masao Matsui's decades in Tokyo, the omakase uses a sesame-and-cottonseed oil blend and the barest whisper of batter: a seasonal soup and sashimi give way to crisp shrimp legs, tender squid, Hokkaido scallop, snow crab wrapped in shiso. A master class in a single technique.

the-four-horsemen-brooklyn-ny.text: The Four Horsemen is the Williamsburg natural-wine bar co-owned by LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy — whose record collection is the soundtrack — that quietly earned a Michelin star. Since 2015, chef Nick Curtola (Camino, Noma, a year in Piedmont) has cooked simple, precise small plates built to flatter one of the city's most influential natural-wine cellars. Casual on its face, exacting in the details — European wine-bar spirit, Brooklyn execution.

torien-new-york-ny.text: Behind blacked-out windows in NoHo, Torien is the New York sibling of Tokyo's one-star Torishiki, bringing master yakitori to a buzzed-in, mysterious counter. Chef Hideo An works the binchotan grill "like a master pianist" — turning, fanning, saucing and brushing — through an omakase of skewers that runs from succulent chicken oysters to crisp vegetables, each kissed with charcoal smoke. Michelin-starred since 2021, precise and singular.

torrisi-new-york-ny.text: Inside Nolita's landmark Puck Building — vaulted ceilings, marble floors, aquamarine velvet — Rich Torrisi's Torrisi is an opulent, Michelin-starred celebration of Italian-American cooking through refined French technique. Its menu is a love letter to New York itself, borrowing from red-sauce joints, Jewish delis, Chinatown and West Indian patty shops: Don's scungilli toast, "cucumbers New Yorkese," cavatelli with spicy Jamaican beef ragù, an elaborate affogato. Glamorous and unmistakably of this city.

tsukimi-new-york-ny.text: Tsukimi — "moon viewing" — is a twelve-seat East Village counter where chef Takanori Akiyama serves a deeply personal, modern kaiseki, its light-bright room of mirrored panels and illuminated ceramics echoing the harvest-moon festival. Guided by the saying "onkochishin," drawing wisdom from tradition to make something new, the seasonal, multi-course tasting unfolds over two-and-a-half to three hours with a thoughtful sake and wine program. Michelin-starred, intimate and quietly poetic.

tuome-new-york-ny.text: Tuome (pronounced "tow-me") is Thomas Chen's East Village pioneer of casual fine dining — a New American room shaded by his Chinese-American roots and Eleven Madison Park training. A former accountant who followed his passion to the stove, Chen earned a Michelin star in 2019 for dishes like octopus with pork XO, chicken-liver mousse with New York maple, crispy deviled eggs, and the fan-favorite "Pig Out for Two" of Berkshire pork and spicy peanut noodles. Relaxed, personal and assured.

yamada-new-york-ny.text: Yamada marks the return of kaiseki master Isao Yamada — former executive chef of the pioneering, Michelin-starred Brushstroke — to a serene Chinatown counter of hinoki wood and kintsugi-inspired black-and-gold marble. Trained in Japan, including at three-star Kitcho, and steeped in the tea ceremony, Yamada centers his ten-course menu on shun (season), chōwa (harmony) and ikigai (mindfulness). Michelin-starred, a wabi-sabi expression of a life's work.

yoshino-new-york-ny.text: On the Bowery, Yoshino is chef Tadashi Yoshida's exacting omakase, named for his father's hometown in Nara — a counter carved from a single 300-year-old hinoki tree. Yoshida ran one of Japan's top-rated sushi restaurants before relocating to New York in 2021, and his roughly twenty-course menu pairs impeccably sourced sushi with an unusual range of cooked dishes. Michelin-starred and ranked No. 1 in North America by Opinionated About Dining in 2025, quietly thrilling.

7-adams-san-francisco-ca.text: 7 Adams is the Fillmore-district sophomore from husband-and-wife chefs David and Serena Chow Fisher — named for David's childhood home in upstate New York, where his family still runs a diner. In an accessible, warm room the couple serve Californian cooking of "signature magic," from kabocha-filled caramelle with chanterelles to crisp-skinned black cod with sunchoke confit and shellfish broth. Michelin-starred in 2024, its menus, five to ten courses, make fine dining feel down to earth.

angler-sf-san-francisco-ca.text: Angler is Joshua Skenes's more relaxed, seafood-driven counterpart to his three-star Saison — a large Embarcadero waterfront room built around a 32-foot wood-burning hearth. Live-fire cooking happens in full view, applied to top-tier product from a small group of local purveyors: a raw bar of oysters, clams and sea urchin, cured amberjack, spot prawns, California king crab, hot grilled rabbit. Michelin-starred, it captures the Pacific in flame and coastal elegance.

auberge-du-soleil-rutherford-ca.text: Perched above the Silverado Trail with sweeping vineyard views, the restaurant at Auberge du Soleil has been a Napa fine-dining landmark since 1981 — the valley's first, and a Michelin star-holder for nearly two decades running. Chef Robert Curry's cooking is the very definition of California cuisine: refined French technique meeting local produce and global accents, from Nantucket Bay scallops in green-garlic sauce to squid-ink linguine with Mendocino uni and A5 wagyu. A deep, grower-focused wine list completes the hillside idyll.

auro-calistoga-ca.text: Inside the Four Seasons Napa Valley, Auro is Calistoga's only Michelin-starred restaurant, which earned its star just eight months after opening in 2022. The kitchen made its name under chef Rogelio Garcia — one of few Mexican chefs to earn a California star — blending classical French technique with Mexican and Japanese influences across a seven-course, Northern-California tasting: a dayboat scallop over koshihikari rice with garlic mojo verde, dry-aged hiramasa with citrus-tamarind aguachile. A Wine Country expression of border-spanning cooking.

bell-s-los-alamos-ca.text: Bell's is a family-run French bistro in tiny Los Alamos, set in a former Bank of Italy building, where James Beard-winning chef Daisy Ryan cooks what she calls "Franch" — French technique loosened up with Santa Barbara County ranch sensibility and local produce. A Food & Wine Best New Chef, Ryan earned a Michelin star for refined-yet-relaxed dishes like wild snails in garlic-parsley butter, a Santa Barbara uni crêpe cake with crème fraîche and caviar, and lamb en croûte over Calabrian-chili aïoli. Approachable, precise, deeply local.

caruso-s-montecito-ca.text: Caruso's sits on the sand at the Rosewood Miramar Beach in Montecito — an oceanfront, al fresco dining room where executive chef Massimo Falsini fuses Southern Italian heritage with California produce. A Michelin star and Green Star reflect its hyper-local ethos: some 90% of seafood sustainably harvested nearby, honey from the property's bees, herbs from a micro-seasonal garden. With Pacific views and a private beachside "Sapore di Stelle" table, it is coastal Italian dining at its most idyllic.

chez-noir-carmel-by-the-sea-ca.text: Chez Noir is the passion project of husband-and-wife team Jonny and Monique Black, set in a converted house in Carmel-by-the-Sea. Chef Jonny Black — a CIA scholarship grad who cooked with Gordon Ramsay, Dominique Crenn and Michael Tusk — earned a Michelin star within months of opening in 2022 for a seafood-centric menu of micro-seasonal Monterey Peninsula ingredients, shaded with French and northern-Spanish influences. "Everyday luxury" with the warmth of a family-run room.

citrin-santa-monica-ca.text: Citrin is Josiah Citrin's more relaxed, à la carte counterpart to his two-star Mélisse, sharing a Santa Monica address with its sibling. Drawing on 25-plus years and an encyclopedic knowledge of California growers, Citrin pairs French technique with peak seasonal produce in a fun, welcoming room with a large bar and a modest prix-fixe. Michelin-starred, it is the approachable half of a two-restaurant institution.

corridor-109-los-angeles-ca.text: Corridor 109 is Brian Baik's eleven-seat counter in Melrose Hill, hidden behind his sister bar — one seating a night, a must-book Michelin star from the 2026 Los Angeles guide. The New-York-honed chef turns dinner into theater: an eleven-course, $325 tasting focused on fish largely sourced from Japan, much of it served raw, with technical precision and seasonal Southern California ingredients. Intimate, paced and contemporary.

cyrus-geyserville-ca.text: Cyrus is the reinvention of Douglas Keane and Nick Peyton's celebrated Healdsburg restaurant, which held two Michelin stars from 2005 to 2012 before a decade-long hiatus; it reopened in a coolly modern concrete-and-glass Geyserville space in 2022 and won a star anew. Dinner is a choreographed journey — Champagne and canapés in the lounge, small bites in the kitchen, substantial courses in the dining room, a finale in the Chocolate Room — rethought around living wages and work/life balance for staff as much as delight for guests.

heritage-long-beach-ca.text: Set in a restored Craftsman home in Long Beach's Rose Park, Heritage is chef Philip Pretty's zero-waste tasting-menu restaurant — Long Beach's first Michelin star, and a Green Star holder — opened in 2020 with his sister Lauren. The frequently changing nine-course menu is line-caught, pasture-raised and market-driven, with every trim repurposed: a box-crab crostada, fig-leaf ice cream with honeycomb, a 32-day-aged Santa Carota rib chop dusted in leek ash. Intentional, elegant and quietly sustainable.

hilda-and-jesse-san-francisco-ca.text: Hilda and Jesse began as a brunch pop-up before landing in North Beach in 2021 — a queer-owned room named for the founders' grandparents and billed as "modern #FunLuxury." Executive chef and partner Ollie K.C. Liedags blends fine-dining technique with playful reinterpretations of the classics, earning a Michelin star in 2024, with a service nod, for whimsical, impeccably sourced plays on avocado toast, buttermilk pancakes and a cheeky "grade school breakfast." Serious cooking that refuses to take itself too seriously.

jeune-et-jolie-carlsbad-ca.text: Jeune et Jolie — "young and beautiful" — is Eric Bost's rose-hued, sunlit French bistro in Carlsbad Village, Michelin-starred since 2021. Guy Savoy-trained, Bost marries nouvelle-French technique with peak Southern California produce and an oyster-focused raw bar across a four-course menu: grilled leeks with buttermilk and black truffle, a decadent croque madame of ibérico ham and Kaluga caviar, sea bass with saffron. Inventive, seasonal and rooted in place.

kali-los-angeles-ca.text: Kali is Kevin Meehan's Hollywood mainstay, Michelin-starred since 2019 — for nearly a decade a Californian tasting-menu destination, and since 2025 reinvented as a refined mid-century steakhouse. Meehan, who honed his craft at L'Orangerie, Bastide and Patina, now pairs perfectly cooked steaks and ice-cold martinis with the same seasonal, artisanal-farm sourcing that built his reputation. Approachable yet exacting, a contemporary Californian take on the American steakhouse.

kin-khao-san-francisco-ca.text: Tucked into an alcove of the Parc 55 hotel, Kin Khao is Pim Techamuanvivit's cult-favorite Thai restaurant — her first U.S. venture, Michelin-starred within eighteen months of its 2014 opening. On a mission to "liberate Thai cuisine from the tyranny of peanut sauce," the Bangkok-born chef cooks vibrant, tradition-rooted dishes with Northern California produce: a fragrant hor mok curry mousse with puffed rice cakes, green curry with local slow-cooked rabbit. Authentic, layered and produce-driven.

kojima-los-angeles-ca.text: On the second floor of a Sawtelle strip mall, KOJIMA is Tokyo-trained chef Hayato Kojima's homey, counter-wrapped omakase — Michelin-starred and one of LA's most compelling new Japanese rooms. Beyond pristine fish flown from Toyosu market, Kojima's kaiseki-inspired, daily-changing menu weaves in vegetables and meticulous hot dishes alongside fresh Southern California ingredients. There is no printed menu; the warm staff narrates each course of a meal dictated purely by the day's sourcing.

lielle-los-angeles-ca.text: Lielle — named for Swedish chef Marcus Jernmark's daughter — is his first stateside restaurant, a cozy, barrel-vaulted Beverlywood room that earned a Michelin star in the 2026 guide. The former Aquavit chef anchors a concise, product-focused tasting in California ingredients and Scandinavian restraint, served family-style rather than formally: agnolotti del plin with Gruyère custard, black truffle and beurre noisette. Refined without stuffiness, warm in its hospitality.

localis-sacramento-ca.text: Localis is a Midtown Sacramento standout — Michelin-starred since 2022 — where chef Christopher Barnum-Dann, a former electrician and musician turned self-taught cook, builds a freewheeling, travel-inspired tasting menu. Thoroughly Californian in its sourcing, it reimagines flavors from his journeys, from Thai beef tartare on tapioca chips to octopus piccata, matched to inventive pairings that won him Michelin's 2025 California Sommelier Award. Imaginative, personal and wine-smart.

lucien-la-jolla-ca.text: Lucien — named for chef Elijah Arizmendi's young son — is a La Jolla tasting-menu newcomer that earned a Michelin star in the 2026 guide. Arizmendi, whose résumé runs through Spago, Per Se, Robuchon and Daniel, celebrates San Diego's farmers and fishermen through French and Japanese technique across a twelve-course menu: San Diego uni with ibérico guanciale and caviar, local yellowtail with morita and pomelo, crisp-skinned tilefish with fennel and pomegranate. Polished, coastal and precise.

madcap-san-anselmo-ca.text: Madcap is Marin County's only Michelin-starred restaurant — chef Ron Siegel's relaxed San Anselmo room, starred since 2019. Siegel, whose three decades span the French Laundry, Aqua and Michael Mina, and who was the first American to beat an Iron Chef on the original show, cooks seasonal modern-American tasting menus with French and Japanese accents and Northern California bounty: tuna tartare with ginger in a rice cracker, charred octopus over fermented pimento, umeboshi with daikon "noodles" and ponzu. Refined but never pretentious.

meteora-los-angeles-ca.text: Meteora is Jordan Kahn's live-fire, rainforest-inspired Melrose restaurant — what the Vespertine and Destroyer chef calls "a 2,000-year-old version of Vespertine." Michelin-starred in 2024, it marries primal open-fire cooking with a zero-waste ethos and wild, organic California ingredients: charred yam with smoked trout roe and grilled hazelnuts, honey-grilled scallops, a caramelized plantain dumpling with huitlacoche. Ancient technique refined through contemporary artistry.

mister-jiu-s-san-francisco-ca.text: In Chinatown's historic Four Seas building, Brandon Jew's Mister Jiu's has reimagined Chinese-American cooking since 2016 — the first Chinese restaurant in San Francisco to earn a Michelin star, held for nearly a decade. Jew fuses Cantonese tradition with California's seasonal bounty: melting scallion milk bread with honey butter, silken tofu with maitake and green Sichuan peppercorn, a signature Peking duck with whipped liver mousse, Dungeness crab cheong fun. A landmark of reinvention.

miura-beverly-hills-ca.text: Above the Two Rodeo galleria in Beverly Hills, Miura is a serene Edomae sushi-kappo counter led by Derek Wilcox — the first and only Westerner to complete a full seven-year apprenticeship at Kyoto's three-star Kikunoi, later trained in Edomae sushi at Ginza Sushi Aoki. Michelin-starred, it flies wild maguro and premium seafood direct from Japan, never farmed, elevating traditional sushi with refined kaiseki and kappo technique. Precise, seasonal and deeply pedigreed.

mori-nozomi-los-angeles-ca.text: Mori Nozomi is chef Nozomi Mori's eight-seat Los Angeles omakase, where an all-female team serves a 22-to-25-course, kaiseki-inflected menu grounded in wabi-sabi. A former fashion-industry professional who trained at the two-star Sushi Ginza Onodera before opening her own room in 2024, Mori folds farmers-market tsukemono, fresh wagashi and seasonal Japanese seafood into a distinctly personal format. Michelin-starred and a New York Times Top 50 pick, a $250 omakase and a trailblazing voice.

n-naka-los-angeles-ca.text: Niki Nakayama's n/naka is Los Angeles's temple of modern kaiseki — a Palms-neighborhood room made famous by Netflix's Chef's Table, on which Nakayama was Season 1's only female chef. Co-owned with her wife and co-chef Carole Iida-Nakayama, the roughly thirteen-course, four-hour kaiseki applies Japanese tradition through a Californian lens, with around 70% of ingredients sourced locally and a months-long waitlist for its 22 seats. Harmony, seasonality and quiet artistry, Michelin-honored.

nari-san-francisco-ca.text: Nari — "women" in Thai — is Pim Techamuanvivit's second Michelin-starred San Francisco restaurant, a tribute to the generations of Thai women cooks at the heart of the cuisine. Opened in 2019, it reimagines traditional Thai flavors through fantastic California ingredients: a brick-red bumbai curry with crispy eggplant and flaky roti, a yum sum-o pomelo salad with crispy shallots, grilled Monterey squid with sticky-sweet pork jowl. Bold, contemporary and personal — the more ambitious sibling to her Kin Khao.

niku-steakhouse-san-francisco-ca.text: Niku Steakhouse marries the American steakhouse with Japanese sensibility — a Michelin-starred SoMa room built around a binchotan-charcoal and wood-fired yakiniku grill, with kappo-style counter seating. Executive chef Dustin Falcon works Northern California terroir and foraged ingredients alongside prime domestic and A5 Japanese wagyu, dry-aged at the adjacent butchery whose head butcher travels to Japan for rarities like olive-fed wagyu. Chawanmushi and maitake confit in wagyu fat round out a serious, seasonally driven steakhouse.

nisei-san-francisco-ca.text: Nisei — the term for American-born children of Japanese immigrants — is chef David Yoshimura's deeply personal Japanese-American restaurant, Michelin-starred since 2022. A wd~50 and Californios alum, Yoshimura reinterprets washoku through his heritage and California ingredients: a buckwheat-potato tartlet with date miso, nori maki of silken tofu and Blue Lake beans with trout roe, Santa Barbara uni in almond dashi foam, an omurice crowned with caviar. Imaginative, refined and rooted in identity.

nozawa-bar-beverly-hills-ca.text: Hidden at the back of a Beverly Hills Sugarfish — and entirely independent of it — Nozawa Bar is a ten-seat "secret sushi" counter, Michelin-starred, opened in 2013 by the Sugarfish team including Kazunori Nozawa. Two seatings a night work through some 22 courses of nigiri, sashimi and hand rolls built on exceptional, largely local seafood. A jewel-box omakase in the heart of the Golden Triangle.

orsa-and-winston-los-angeles-ca.text: Orsa & Winston is Josef Centeno's intimate downtown LA fusion of Italian and Japanese sensibilities — a Michelin-starred, minimalist room serving a nightly-changing omakase tasting. The San Antonio-born chef, who reshaped DTLA dining with Bäco Mercat and Bar Amá, sends out signatures like a satsuki rice porridge with parmesan cream and uni, and squid-ink spaghetti with Maine lobster and momotaro tomato. An LA Times restaurant of the year, quietly inventive.

osteria-mozza-los-angeles-ca.text: Nancy Silverton's Osteria Mozza has anchored Hollywood since 2007 — a Michelin-starred, Green-Star Italian celebrated above all for its mozzarella bar, where the James Beard-winning chef reinvented antipasti and "perfected the art of cheese." Beyond smoked mozzarella with parma ham, the menu runs to handmade pasta, from pappardelle with rabbit ragù to an oxtail-ragù pasta, plus grilled octopus and crispy duck confit. Traditional, seasonal Italian cooking from one of America's most influential chefs.

pasta-bar-encino-ca.text: Tucked into an Encino strip mall, Pasta|Bar is a Michelin-starred, eighteen-seat tasting-menu counter from Phillip Frankland Lee and Margarita Kallas-Lee's Scratch Restaurants — pasta pushed far past tradition. Chef DJ Nelson walks diners through each course of a $245 menu built on handmade pastas and hyper-local ingredients: a king-crab raviolo with fermented pineapple and macadamia, cavatelli with ibérico pork and mole, a bone-marrow custard dessert. Intimate, personal and inventive.

plumed-horse-saratoga-ca.text: A Saratoga landmark since 1952, the Plumed Horse has held a Michelin star every year since 2008 under chef-owner Peter Armellino. A Gramercy Tavern alum with 35-plus years behind him, Armellino cooks modern Californian fare from a local farm's hand-picked produce — his signature black-pepper-parmesan soufflé with uni and blue-crab fondue among them — paired from a 20,000-bottle, Wine Spectator Grand Award cellar. Refined Silicon Valley fine dining with deep roots.

press-saint-helena-ca.text: PRESS is a St. Helena celebration of Napa Valley — its people, produce and wine — reinvigorated by chef-partner Philip Tessier, who earned it a Michelin star in 2022. Long a steak house, it now balances dry-aged American wagyu and côte de boeuf with modern, refined plates: Kusshi oysters with whipped horseradish, a lobster bisque with scallop croquette, ricotta gnudi with hazelnut. It also holds the world's largest collection of Napa Valley wines — over 2,700 selections going back seven decades.

protege-palo-alto-ca.text: Protégé is the Palo Alto restaurant of two French Laundry alums — chef Anthony Secviar, also of Akelarre and El Bulli, and master sommelier Dennis Kelly — bringing three-star polish to a relaxed setting. Michelin-starred, it splits into a casual à la carte Lounge and a Dining Room serving a seven-course tasting: Pacific sablefish in sweet-onion dashi, a nine-layer morel lasagna with Madeira, Flannery beef with green-garlic gnocchi. Fine-dining rigor, Silicon Valley ease, and a serious wine and spirits program.

restaurant-ki-los-angeles-ca.text: Restaurant Ki made history as the first Korean restaurant in Los Angeles to earn a Michelin star — a twelve-seat Little Tokyo counter that took its star in the same year it opened, 2025. Chef Ki Kim, a Jungsik and Atomix alum and Michelin's 2025 Young Chef Award winner, threads nostalgic Korean flavor through avant-garde California technique: shirako gimbap with truffle rice and kimchi, perilla-seed pasta with winter truffle, barbecue squab with foie gras sauce, 45-day dry-aged dairy cow with Korean bone broth. Groundbreaking and assured.

restaurant-naides-san-francisco-ca.text: Restaurant Naides is the Bay Area's first Filipino tasting-menu restaurant — a Nob Hill jewel box named for chef Patrick Gabon's mother, and Michelin-starred. Gabon, who cooked at O' by Claude Le Tohic and Sons & Daughters, and partner Celine Wuu, a Benu veteran, weave Filipino flavors and California ingredients through the New Nordic techniques of pickling, fermenting, foraging and curing that Gabon found echoed his homeland's cooking. A brioche "pandesal" with braised chicken gizzards riffs on sisig; dry-aged duck "adobo" meets soy jus and horseradish; whole courses honor a single ingredient like the fermented shrimp paste bagoong. Modern, personal Filipino fine dining.

r-o-rebel-omakase-laguna-beach-ca.text: R|O-Rebel Omakase is Laguna Beach's first Michelin-starred restaurant — an understated counter where chef Jordan Nakasone oversees two reservation-only seatings a night. The tightly focused omakase balances seasonality and top-quality product, with skillfully prepared nigiri showcasing delicacies like yagara (red cornetfish) and nodoguro (blackthroat sea perch), plus kitchen dishes with a bit of flair. Intimate, precise Edomae sushi on the Orange County coast.
